questions.enonce_markdown:
Identify and explain the fallacies clearly committed in the following statements.
(i) The senior prefect of G.H.S Nem was summoned to face the disciplinary council for extorting gifts and money from students through intimidation, when interrogated, he exclaimed "oh well, the principal as well collects bribe from parents during the admission of new students into the institution."
(ii) The Managing Director of one credit union instructed his account officer "Record these bills under the company's account, else you will lose your job."
(iii) Since the code of conduct stipulates that all teachers should go to school and teach their students, Mr. Tabe, a Philosophy teacher, sick of Tuberculosis must go to school and teach.
(3 x 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Tu quoque ("you too"), a form of ad hominem circumstantial.**
The prefect does not answer the charge of extortion; he points to another person's misconduct (the principal's alleged bribe-taking) as if it excused or cancelled his own. Even if the principal does take bribes, that is a separate wrong: it neither proves that the prefect is innocent nor justifies his conduct ("two wrongs make a right"). The attack on the accuser's side shifts attention from the issue to someone else's character.

**(ii) Argumentum ad baculum (appeal to force or threat).**
The Managing Director gives no reason why the bills should be recorded under the company's account; he replaces reasons by a threat ("else you will lose your job"). The officer is pushed to accept the instruction because of the penalty, not because the instruction is justified (it is, besides, an invitation to falsify accounts). Fear is used instead of evidence.

**(iii) Fallacy of accident (dicto simpliciter, or sweeping generalisation).**
A general rule ("all teachers should go to school and teach") is applied to a particular case without regard to exceptional circumstances: Mr. Tabe is sick of tuberculosis, which is serious and contagious, so he needs treatment and could endanger his pupils and himself. General rules carry implicit exceptions; to conclude that he "must" teach regardless of his illness is to apply the rule where its conditions do not hold.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Translate the following arguments into valid standard forms; indicate their validity or invalidity, moods and mood names.
(i) Some philosophers are not theologians; some intellectuals are not theologians; All philosophers are intellectuals. (3 marks)
(ii) Some housewives are mothers; some enduring persons are mothers; All housewives are enduring persons. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
In each argument the last proposition, introduced as the conclusion, is the proposition to be established; the other two are the premises. A standard-form syllogism states the major premise (the one containing the predicate of the conclusion, the major term $P$) first, then the minor premise (containing the subject of the conclusion, the minor term $S$), then the conclusion. The mood is the sequence of the three letters A, E, I, O and the figure is fixed by the position of the middle term $M$.

**(i)** $S$ = philosophers, $P$ = intellectuals, $M$ = theologians.

> Some intellectuals are not theologians. (Some $P$ are not $M$): O
> Some philosophers are not theologians. (Some $S$ are not $M$): O
> Therefore, all philosophers are intellectuals. (All $S$ are $P$): A

Mood **OOA**, figure 2 (the middle term is the predicate of both premises): **OOA-2**. The argument is **invalid**, and no traditional mood name exists for it (only valid moods have names). Rules broken:

- two negative premises (exclusive premises);
- an affirmative conclusion drawn from negative premises;
- two particular premises;
- illicit minor: "philosophers" is distributed in the universal conclusion but undistributed in the minor premise.

Counter-example: let there be no theologians, intellectuals = $\{a\}$ and philosophers = $\{a, b\}$. Both premises are true, but $b$ is a philosopher who is not an intellectual, so the conclusion is false. (Checked by computer search over all models.)

**(ii)** $S$ = housewives, $P$ = enduring persons, $M$ = mothers.

> Some enduring persons are mothers. (Some $P$ are $M$): I
> Some housewives are mothers. (Some $S$ are $M$): I
> Therefore, all housewives are enduring persons. (All $S$ are $P$): A

Mood **IIA**, figure 2: **IIA-2**. The argument is **invalid**; it has no mood name. Rules broken:

- undistributed middle: "mothers" is the predicate of two I propositions and is never distributed;
- illicit minor: "housewives" is distributed in the conclusion but not in the minor premise;
- two particular premises, and a universal conclusion drawn from particular premises.

Counter-example: mothers = $\{a\}$, enduring persons = $\{a\}$, housewives = $\{a, b\}$: both premises true, conclusion false because $b$ is a housewife who is not an enduring person. (Checked by computer search over all models.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Using p, q, r, and s, symbolise the following statements:
(i) It will rain today if and only if the weather is dull, although it is not absolutely true.
(ii) Neither Lucifer nor his agents are powerful; nevertheless, God is giving them more time to repent from their evil ways.
(iii) If teachers are gardeners, then learners are plants, however, the absence of the gardeners implies the disappearance of the plants.
(3 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
In symbolisation, "although", "nevertheless" and "however" are translated as a conjunction ("and"), "if and only if" as the biconditional $\equiv$, "implies" and "if... then" as the conditional $\supset$, and "neither... nor" as the negation of a disjunction.

**(i)** $p$ = it will rain today; $q$ = the weather is dull; $r$ = it is absolutely true (that it will rain today if and only if the weather is dull).

$$(p \equiv q) \cdot \sim r$$

**(ii)** $p$ = Lucifer is powerful; $q$ = Lucifer's agents are powerful; $r$ = God is giving them more time to repent from their evil ways.

$$\sim(p \vee q) \cdot r$$

(equivalent to $\sim p \cdot \sim q \cdot r$ by De Morgan's law).

**(iii)** $p$ = teachers are gardeners; $q$ = learners are plants; $r$ = the gardeners are absent; $s$ = the plants disappear.

$$(p \supset q) \cdot (r \supset s)$$

questions.enonce_markdown:
Construct a truth table to determine whether the statements below are Contingent, Tautologous or Contradictory.
(i) [(M.K) ⊃ (M v K)]
(ii) ~(B ⊃ D) . D
(2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** $(M \cdot K) \supset (M \vee K)$

| $M$ | $K$ | $M \cdot K$ | $M \vee K$ | $(M \cdot K) \supset (M \vee K)$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| T | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | F | T | T |
| F | T | F | T | T |
| F | F | F | F | T |

The last column is true in every row: the statement is a **tautology** (tautologous). Reason: when $M \cdot K$ is true, both $M$ and $K$ are true, so $M \vee K$ is true too; when $M \cdot K$ is false the conditional is true.

**(ii)** $\sim(B \supset D) \cdot D$

| $B$ | $D$ | $B \supset D$ | $\sim(B \supset D)$ | $\sim(B \supset D) \cdot D$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| T | T | T | F | F |
| T | F | F | T | F |
| F | T | T | F | F |
| F | F | T | F | F |

The last column is false in every row: the statement is a **contradiction** (contradictory). Reason: $\sim(B \supset D)$ is true only when $B$ is true and $D$ is false, which is incompatible with the second conjunct $D$.

Neither statement is contingent.
